newsitem.title: USA: Reynolds to sell mill to Alcoa.
newsitem.headline: Reynolds to sell mill to Alcoa.

text.p: Reynolds Metals Co said Monday it has signed a letter of intent to sell a North Alabama rolling mill to Aluminum Co of America.
While terms of the transaction were not disclosed, Reynolds said it expects to realize an after tax loss in the range of $225 to $335 million, or $3.10 to $3.45 per share.

Closing of the transaction is anticipated in the second half of the year, the company said, noting it is subject to regulatory and board approvals, negotiation of definitive agreements and other customary conditions.
Reynolds Metals also said it has determined, as a reult of a previously announced review, that certain plants and businesses no longer strategically fit.
"We are in the process of addressing these plants and businesses, and are proceeding with several favorable opportunities," its statement said.
Reynolds said it will provide a comprehensive report on the results of its portfolio review when it announces second quarter results.
The company said it has closed the sale of its residential construction products business to AmeriMark Inc.

Reynolds said it has signed letters of intent to sell its Bellwood, Va., aluminum reclamation plant to Philip Environmental Inc, its El Campo, Texas, aluminum extrusion plant to a Tredegar Industries Inc subsidiary, and its McCook sheet and plant and Bellwood extrusion plants to Kaiser Aluminum Corp.
The company said these sales are expected to close in the second quarter.
Chairman Jeremiah Sheehan told last week's annual meeting the planned sales are expected to result in undisclosed gains.
The company reported a gain on the sale to AmeriMark in the first quarter.

Assets included in the sale to Alcoa are the Reynolds Alloys rolling mill, two nearby reclamation plants that provide input metal to the mill, and the Sheffield coil coating facility. The principal product manufactured by Reynolds there is aluminum sheet used to produce beverage cans and ends, primarily for use by Reynolds can plants, the company said.
"This asset sale is part of Reynolds' strategy to streamline its business focus. We have traditionally been a higher-cost producer of can sheet and have not been able to close the gap," Sheehan said.
"We believe we will be able to generate better returns for our stockholders by concentrating our resources in areas where we have, or can achieve, a competitive advantage," he explained.
Upon closing, Reynolds and Alcoa plan to enter into a long-term, market-based agreement under which Alcoa will become a major supplier of Reynolds aluminum can sheet requirements, Reynolds said.
"Reynolds anticipates that future employment levels at the plant will be reduced, perhaps substantially, but at this time it is premature to project by how much," said Sheehan.
The four operations now employ about 2,250, it said.
